items.definition: Attention, affection and gifts given far faster and further than the situation deserves.
items.example: The love bombing was hard to refuse: every message came with a declaration.

items.definition: A repeated attack on a person's memory and judgement, so that they stop trusting what they remember.
items.example: It was gaslighting: she was told her own account of the meeting was wrong.

items.definition: A small, easy agreement that is used later as the reason for a much larger one.
items.example: The free trial was the foot in the door: the yearly contract came next.

items.definition: Being cut off from other people without choosing it, and without the comfort that solitude brings.
items.example: Working from home every day turned into isolation by February.

items.definition: Pressure strong enough to take away a person's freedom to decide, in the sense used in law and in medical consent.
items.example: The form said the signature was voluntary; the manager's tone made that undue influence.

items.definition: One move made to push a decision, such as a deadline, a discount or a display of authority.
items.example: The second call was a pressure tactic: it moved the deadline by one hour.

items.definition: Everyone agreeing freely to something, every time. A clear no is a complete answer that needs no follow-up.
items.example: Consent has to be clear on both sides, and a no is always a complete answer.

items.definition: A line you draw around your time, energy, body or values, and say out loud so other people can respect it.
items.example: Her boundary was simple: no phone calls after ten.

items.definition: A pattern in which one person keeps control over another by limiting their money, their time or their contact with other people.
items.example: The pattern of coercive control is recognised by what it restricts, not by what it says.

items.definition: Using external tools to store, compute or retrieve information so that your own mind does not have to.
The shared system by which a group, or a person and a tool, divides the work of remembering who knows what.
The disciplined practice of examining claims, evidence and reasoning before accepting a conclusion.
The ability to form, hold and explain your own views without needing them to be pre-approved by an authority or a tool.
The gradual loss of a skill when it is no longer practiced because a machine performs it instead.
The weakening of mental abilities through long disuse, similar to the shrinking of an unexercised muscle.
The capacity to direct one's own thinking: forming, testing and owning one's judgments rather than receiving them.
The power to act deliberately and be responsible for one's actions, as opposed to reacting or being acted upon.
The obligation to stand behind one's beliefs and claims: to have checked them and to correct them when wrong.
The habits that keep a person's information environment healthy: limits, filters, sources and offline time.
The continuous practice of building and refreshing one's knowledge and skills throughout life.
Thinking about one's own thinking: noticing how one learns, decides, and errs.
The work of knowing one field deeply instead of many fields broadly.
items.example: Specialisation is why the same engineer finds a fault in ten minutes that takes another person a day.

items.definition: A person whose work is in one field and who is trusted to judge work in that field.
items.example: She is the specialist for the pump, so she read the report in ten minutes.

items.definition: The area of work that a person, a document or a decision covers.
items.example: The scope of this decision covers the money, the contract and the customer.

items.definition: The ability to do a piece of work well.
items.example: His competence is in the numbers; the rest of the project is not his field.

items.definition: A part of a situation that a person cannot see well, because of what the person already knows.
items.example: Her blind spot is the customer: the figure was right and nobody asked who was waiting for the machine.

items.definition: The ability to form an opinion from experience and to defend it.
items.example: The judgement to stop the line is part of what the company pays for.

items.definition: A habit of attention that leans one way, often without the person noticing.
items.example: The bias is not against the customer; it is away from the customer.

items.definition: Something a plan takes as true without checking it.
items.example: The hidden assumption is that the machine will be ready on the first day.

items.definition: An area of work that a person knows well enough to work in.
items.example: His field is tax, so read the customs part with somebody else.

items.definition: The checking of a thing against a source before it is trusted.
items.example: Verification of the cost is done by finance, not by the person who wrote the estimate.

items.definition: The judgement of a second person, asked because the first one may not see everything.
items.example: Before we sign, I would like a second opinion from somebody outside this field.

items.definition: The passing of work from one person to another.
items.example: At the handover she asked what the customer had actually agreed to.

items.definition: A person who works across several fields and can explain one of them to another.
items.example: The generalist on the team translated the tax rule into plain words.

items.definition: Building software by prompting an AI and accepting generated code based on whether it seems to work, without necessarily understanding it.
The future cost of shortcuts in software: work that must be redone because quick solutions were chosen over correct ones.
The high-level structure of a system: how its parts are divided and connected, decided before the details are written.
The practice of having code read and checked by another developer — or by its author with fresh eyes — before it is accepted.
How easily software can be understood, fixed and extended by a human in the future.
The underlying reason a problem exists, as opposed to the symptom that made it visible.
